title: Dostoevsky's Crime and Punishment
objective: After this level you can explain how Crime and Punishment turns a murder into a psychological drama of guilt and conscience.
summary: In Dostoyevsky's Crime and Punishment (1866), a poor student kills a pawnbroker to prove a theory. The real drama is his guilt: Porfiry's mind games, Sonya's persuasion, confession and Siberia.

cards.headline: A poor student kills an old pawnbroker. Then the real story starts.
cards.body: Fyodor Dostoyevsky's Crime and Punishment, first published in 1866, follows what comes after the crime: Raskolnikov's descent into psychological torment.

cards.headline: A theory that permits a crime
cards.body: Raskolnikov, an impoverished former student in St. Petersburg, decides to solve his problems at a stroke by murdering an old pawnbroker. He has a theory to back it: extraordinary people must have "the right to transgress," or progress would be impossible. The rest of the book puts that theory on trial, inside his own head.

cards.headline: Cat and mouse
cards.body: The detective Porfiry Petrovich guesses who did it but can't prove it, so he plays psychological games instead. Raskolnikov does half the work for him: conscience and mounting suspicion wear him down. The chase happens in conversations, not in alleys. You know who did it from the start; the suspense is whether he will crack.

cards.headline: Confession and Siberia
cards.body: His way out comes through Sonya. She persuades Raskolnikov to confess, and she follows him to Siberia. Even there he clings at first to his theories; repentance comes slowly. By the end, the punishment in the title means much more than a prison sentence.

cards.headline: Crime and Punishment: confessed
learned: Raskolnikov kills to prove a theory

questions.prompt: What did Raskolnikov's theory claim extraordinary people must have?

options.label: A duty to obey every law
A fortune to give away
options.rationale: His motive was his own problems.

questions.explanation: Raskolnikov theorized that extraordinary people must have "the right to transgress," or progress would be impossible.

questions.prompt: How does Porfiry Petrovich pursue Raskolnikov without proof?

options.label: He plays psychological games with him
He plants false evidence at the scene
He pays Sonya to spy on him

questions.explanation: Porfiry guesses Raskolnikov's guilt but cannot prove it, so he plays psychological games with him.

questions.prompt: A fable in Level 2 states its moral, often at the end. Where does Crime and Punishment put Raskolnikov's reckoning instead?

options.label: In a moral printed on the last page
options.rationale: The novel doesn't spell it out.

options.label: Inside his own mind, in guilt and suspicion

questions.explanation: The novel's reckoning is psychological: conscience and mounting suspicion wear Raskolnikov down long before any court.
